Comparison with other BPMN engines

When the process model contains multiple tasks, timers, and gateway logic, database and coordination overheads dominate. Below we contrast sustained, realistic workloads and consider resources required to reach the reported numbers.

TaktX (this report).

  • Model: 10 service tasks (200 ms each), 2×1-minute timers, 1 gateway
  • Cluster: DigitalOcean managed Kafka 3×2 vCPU (RF=2); engines: 1–2 nodes, 4 vCPU each; workers/starter: 4 vCPU.
  • Result: ~850 PI/s (1 node) → ~1,700 PI/s (2 nodes) with p95 < 500 ms, up to ~2M concurrent instances; near-linear scaling from one to two engine nodes.

Camunda / Zeebe “typical” in practice (community evidence).

In field reports for Camunda, realistic models with timers and external tasks frequently plateau around ~30–40 PI/s unless significantly larger clusters and heavy tuning are applied. This aligns with the known cost of job executor/database contention on such workloads.

Context & normalization: Against that backdrop, TaktX’s ~850–1,700 PI/s on small engine nodes and a tiny Kafka cluster represents a 20–50× uplift in sustained throughput for “typical” models, with sub-second p95 latency.

Flowable 6.3.0 – oﬃcial benchmark (public).

Flowable published a performance benchmark showing “close to 10,000 process instances per second (9,541 to be precise), each one executing 10 service tasks” on AWS. This is a light per-instance workload (no minute-long timers and no intentional 200 ms task delays), but it is still a useful public reference for realistic multi-task models.

Context & normalization: My TaktX raw test (no waits) exceeds 100,000 PI/s, i.e., >10× Flowable’s figure on modest hardware; on the typical test (with two minute-level timers and 200 ms workers), TaktX still sustains ~1.7k PI/s on two 4-vCPU nodes — despite the much heavier per-instance work. (Flowable’s post does not include long timers or fixed per-task delays.)

jBPM

jBPM publishes base performance numbers measured through KIE Server, which means results include network and marshalling overhead in addition to the engine itself. Their page reports throughput scaling with client threads, e.g. ~91 process instances/sec with 1 thread and ~240 instances/sec with 4 threads (with further gains at higher thread counts on that page).

How this maps to our “typical” model:

My sustained test (10 service tasks at 200 ms each, two 1-minute timers, gateway) reaches ~850 PI/s on one 4-vCPU engine node and ~1,700 PI/s on two nodes, with p95 < 500 ms and ≈2 M concurrent instances—despite much heavier per-instance work and end-to-end durability (acks=all, idempotent, broadcast updates).

Even allowing for KIE Server overhead in jBPM’s numbers, the order-of-magnitude gap remains:

TaktX delivers significantly higher sustained PI/s on modest hardware for realistic, timer-rich flows.

Notes on comparability: jBPM’s published tests are executed over KIE Server (remote calls +marshalling), whereas my runs use a Kafka-backed architecture with workers and timers inside themodel. The raw numbers aren’t apples-to-apples, but normalizing for resources and model weight still shows a substantial advantage for TaktX on sustained “typical” workloads

Takeaway (typical-process focus):

Throughput per node / per vCPU: TaktX delivers ≈850 PI/s per 4-vCPU engine node on a heavy, timer-rich model — with durability (acks=all, idempotent producers) and exports on. Infra required to reach target rates: Where other engines often require larger broker fleets or beefy DB tiers to stay above a few dozen PI/s on realistic models, TaktX hits ~1.7k PI/s on two small nodes plus a 3-broker Kafka.

Latency under load: TaktX maintains p95 < 500 ms until saturation, whereas forum evidence for other engines shows latency pressure already in the tens of PI/s.

Notes on comparability. No two public benchmarks are perfectly identical. Flowable’s 6.3.0 test uses 10 service tasks but no minute-level timers and no enforced per-task delays; Camunda forum figures reflect real installations rather than staged lab runs. The comparisons above therefore normalize qualitatively for model weight and resources rather than claiming strict apples-to-apples parity. Still, the magnitude of the deltas is clear.
